newsitem.title: RWANDA: Aid workers wait to cross into Zaire's Goma.
newsitem.headline: Aid workers wait to cross into Zaire's Goma.

text.p: Aid workers and supplies queued up at Rwanda's border with Zaire on Monday, waiting for Zairean rebels to allow them to cross into the eastern city of Goma.

But aid officials said even if the first sizeable convoy was allowed into rebel-held Goma it remained doubtful they could reach many of more than one million refugees scattered across eastern Zaire and widely feared to be dying in their thousands.

"We are simply demanding access with good security to the camps so we can carry out an assessment mission impartially," said Marc Gastelleu-Etchegorry of Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF-Doctors Without Borders) as he waited on the Zaire border.
Most of the refugee camps in eastern Zaire have been emptied by a three-week-old rebellion and by former Rwandan Hutu troops and militiamen who have herded camp inmates deeper into Zaire.
Rebel forces who seized Goma a week ago have been unable to push west because of firing, including mortar bombs slamming into the city, from exiled Rwandan Hutu forces around Mugunga refugee camp.

"It's not just an assessment mission. We are taking in medical and logistic supplies and as one of the main problems will be dehydration we are taking in lots of liquids," said Rebecca Trafford-Roberts of the British medical agency Merlin.

A truck from the U.N. Children's Fund, two Save the Children vehicles, two MSF vehicles, two Merlin Land Rovers and one vehicle from a German aid agency lined up on the Rwandan side of the border on Monday.
The Rwandan government, which supports the revolt in eastern Zaire, agreed on Sunday to allow food and medicine into Goma.
Standing on the Rwandan side of the border crossing, Rwandan Health Minister Joseph Kalemera said on Monday: "The bulk of the aid (for refugees) should be delivered on this side and not in Zaire.

"We are giving permission for these vehicles to cross, we have cleared them. But we do not know if there will be problems the other side. We are not capable of putting pressure on the Zaireans in Zairean territory," the Rwandan minister added.
MSF spokeswoman Samantha Bolton said MSF assessment teams were stranded at Gisenyi and at the Ugandan border with Zaire.
In the southern Rwandan town of Cyangugu, teams had not even been allowed to leave the town centre for the border crossing into the rebel-held eastern Zairean town of Bukavu, she added.
Rebels ordered about 30 foreign journalists out of Goma late on Sunday and into western Rwanda, citing security concerns.
Journalists said they were told to go back to Gisenyi by a rebel commander, who gave his name as Commandant Joseph and said they would be allowed to return to eastern Zaire on Monday.

With plans for a multinational intervention force on hold, U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali on Sunday made a new appeal for immediate world intervention to help the refugees, saying thousands were dying with every passing hour.
"Two years ago the international community was confronted by a genocide of the Tutsis by arms. Today we are confronted by a genocide of the Hutus by famine," he said on his way to Rome.
More than a million Hutu refugees fled Rwanda in 1994 fearing reprisals after Hutu hardliners massacred up to a million minority Tutsis and their Hutu sympathisers.

They fled once again when ethnic Tutsis, many of whom have lived in Zaire for generations, launched a revolt near the border with Burundi just over three weeks ago. The rebels now control most towns in the eastern refugee provinces.
Hundreds of thousands of Hutus from Burundi and displaced Zaireans have also fled the fighting. The whereabouts of many in the sprawling and chaotic Central African nation is unknown.
Zaire accuses the Tutsi-dominated Rwandan army of invading its territory. Rwanda accuses Zaire of backing Hutu hardliners who lived among the refugees and launched cross-border raids.
But both Zaire and Rwanda say they want the refugees to go home.

EU Humanitarian Commissioner Emma Bonino held talks with Zaire's government on Sunday and said any refugee return had to be voluntary. "I am opposed to any forced repatriation," she told reporters in Kinshasa.

Earlier, U.N. special envoy Raymond Chretien failed to win Zairean support for safe havens inside Zaire. "It's extremely frustrating for me to see more obstacles presenting themselves than possible solutions," he said in Kinshasa.
He later flew to Rwanda's capital Kigali, saying he wanted to narrow wide-ranging differences between Zaire and Rwanda and underpin a rebel ceasefire, which has been widely violated.
